content: Hypoglycaemia is a frequent condition in individuals with diabetes, but it can also occur in non-diabetic individuals due to disruptions in glucose homeostasis. The optimal method for administering glucose in first aid situations for suspected hypoglycaemia remains unclear. This study aimed to evaluate the effects of glucose administration via various enteral routes suitable for first-aid providers, including buccal, sublingual, oral, and rectal routes. A systematic search was conducted across multiple databases, including CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, and CINAHL, as well as grey literature sources such as the WHO ICTRP Search Portal, ClinicalTrials.gov, and the EU Clinical Trials Register, up to July 2018. Studies involving adults, children with documented or suspected hypoglycaemia, and healthy volunteers were included. Data were extracted and analyzed using rigorous methodologies, including the Cochrane 'Risk of bias' tool for randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and the ROBINS-I tool for non-randomized studies. Continuous outcomes were reported as mean differences (MD) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs), and dichotomous outcomes were reported as risk ratios (RR) with 95% CIs. All glucose concentration data were standardized to mg/dL. From 6394 references, four studies involving 77 participants were included. These studies examined three glucose administration routes: sublingual, buccal, and a combination of oral and buccal administration. All studies exhibited a high risk of bias in at least one domain. 1. Sublingual Administration: In children with hypoglycaemia and concurrent malaria or respiratory tract infections, sublingual administration of table sugar resulted in a higher blood glucose concentration after 20 minutes compared to oral administration (MD 17 mg/dL, 95% CI 4.4 to 29.6; P = 0.008; 1 study; 42 participants). The resolution of hypoglycaemia at 80 minutes appeared to favor sublingual administration (RR 2.10, 95% CI 1.24 to 3.54; P = 0.006; 1 study; 42 participants), but no significant difference was observed at 20 minutes (RR 1.26, 95% CI 0.91 to 1.74; P = 0.16; 1 study; 42 participants). Sublingual administration also reduced the time to resolution of hypoglycaemia (MD -51.5 minutes, 95% CI -58 to -45; P < 0.001; 1 study; 42 participants). No adverse events were reported. However, the evidence quality was very low due to the small sample size and methodological limitations. 2. Buccal Administration: In one study, buccal administration resulted in a lower plasma glucose concentration after 20 minutes compared to oral administration (MD -14.4 mg/dL, 95% CI -17.5 to -11.4; P < 0.001; 1 trial; 16 participants). Another study found fewer participants with increased blood glucose levels at 20 minutes when using buccal administration compared to oral administration (RR 0.07, 95% CI 0.00 to 0.98; P = 0.05; 1 study; 7 participants). No data were available regarding symptom resolution, time to resolution, adverse events, or treatment delays. The evidence quality was very low. 3. Combined Oral and Buccal Administration (Dextrose Gel): In one study, the combined oral and buccal route using dextrose gel did not demonstrate a significant difference in plasma glucose concentration compared to oral administration of glucose tablets or solutions (MD -15.3 mg/dL, 95% CI -33.6 to 3; P = 0.09; 1 study; 18 participants). No improvement was observed in symptom resolution at 20 minutes or less (RR 0.36, 95% CI 0.12 to 1.14; P = 0.08; 1 study; 18 participants). No data were available for time to symptom resolution, hypoglycaemia resolution, adverse events, or treatment delays. The evidence quality was very low. In conclusion, oral glucose administration appears to result in higher blood glucose concentrations after 20 minutes compared to buccal administration. Sublingual sugar administration may be more effective in raising blood glucose levels in children with hypoglycaemia and concurrent malaria or respiratory illness, but these findings are based on very low-quality evidence. The combined oral and buccal route using dextrose gel did not show significant advantages over oral glucose administration. These results should be interpreted with caution due to the limited number of participants, the small number of studies, and methodological weaknesses in the included research.
